In June / July 2013, posts started coming up accusing the owners of Quickmeme of vote manipulation. Quickmeme received a site-wide Reddit ban pretty quickly, and Imgur launched a meme / macro generator just a day or two later.

I'm not implying that dank memes are serious business, but given Reddit and Imgur's ties, and their cooperation in phasing out FPH, it just got me thinking. I was as skeptical of everything I saw at the time, but the quickness with how they moved on Quickmeme and the rise of its replacements seemed really fishy.

I'm not sure how to archive stuff, but if you google "Quickmeme Reddit Scandal" you can find the original post. This article explains Imgur's implementation of a generator, and has some informational links, too: http://www.techspot.com/news/53078-imgur-launches-its-own-meme-generator-amid-quickmeme-scandal.html
Has anyone ever been curious about the Quickmeme scandal?

Quickmeme was in the process of being sold to 9gag at the time. The deal was already set in stone mere days before the vote manipulation scandal saw the light of day.

Quickmeme was in the top 500 sites in the entire world at the time, according to alexa rankings. This means 9gag had to spend millions of dollars to buy Quickmeme. They fully expected that the site was a smash hit and that it was sure to be a sound investment.

Just days after the sale completed, though, Quickmeme was banned from reddit, and so all of the traffic that used to go to them now went to imgur instead. Quickmeme's traffic and alexa ranking permanently dropped like a rock overnight, and 9gag lost millions of dollars on a turd of a site.

How does the vote scandal fit into this? Well, the creator of Quickmeme was running vote bots to give every Quickmeme submission in AdviceAnimals 6 extra upvotes right after being submitted. It also gave 6 extra downvotes to everything else, such as imgur and other competing meme sites. This was enough to cause Quickmeme to take up 99% of the visible submissions in AdviceAnimals, which was a default subreddit at the time. This meant they got a TON of constant traffic to their site.

This manipulation was happening for over a year. What should raise eyebrows is that the reddit admins were notified multiple times by ManWithoutModem during that year. (ManWithoutModem was a moderator of AdviceAnimals who noticed something fishy was happening). But each time he brought it up to the admins, they "looked into it" and determined that nothing was happening and that he was imagining everything.

This is incredibly suspicious, because the admins would have easily been able to confirm within seconds that the same 6 accounts with the same 6 IPs were voting in unison on everything in the subreddit for a solid year. It would have been IMPOSSIBLE for them to miss. In fact, they should have automatically detected it before anyone ever alerted them to it.

Occam's razor therefore dictates that the admins not only knew the manipulation was happening, but they were happy to help cover it up and to allow it to continue. And the only reason for them to do THAT is if they had something to gain from it. Hence, it is incredibly likely that some reddit admins got a cut of the Quickmeme sale price after helping to artificially inflate the perceived value of the site into the millions of dollars range.

It's beyond suspicious that imgur had a replacement meme generator ready to go just days after Quickmeme was banned, too. And oh how very convenient that the vote scandal could be pinned on this random site owner who vanished into the shadows never to be seen on the internet again, rather than blamed on the reddit admins who helped to orchestrate the whole thing and whose careers would be at stake if they were implicated.

Even though imgur had a meme generator ready to go after Quickmeme was banned, a ton of replacement meme sites sprung up at the same time like memedad, makeameme, livememe, imgflip, etc. People liked those sites too, and they were dilluting the influence imgur had on AdviceAnimals. Reddit wanted to reign in how much traffic went to those other image hosts, but they knew it would start a shitstorm from the ethics crowd if they banned a bunch of meme sites that did nothing wrong. So they simply removed AdviceAnimals from the default subreddits, under the false pretense that "well, nobody wants to look at dank memes, they'd rather see TwoXChromosomes instead" (lol wut). That way, barely anyone would see those alternative sites anymore, the sheep would stay herded onto imgur, and nobody could cry foul about it.

You're already trialing a partnership scheme with creators of original content. But I think another way to go about it would be to encourage the creation subverses where people would want to post, even if they weren't paid to do it.
